I'm new here, but I will answer your question.
I worked part-time for two years in human resources.
The first thing is experience. If you have experience, you are almost surely hired.
The second thing was academics. High academic results usually show adaptability. Very high academics is your way out if you don't have XP.
The third one was trickier. We looked for emotionally stable people. The emotionally stable are predictable workers and don't cause problems of almost any kind. We had a low budget, so we had to figure out how to do this. We figured it out that hate trumps love because it is the strongest feeling, and therefore, inherently subjective. We asked the candidates trick questions "do you hate X, Y and Z, being woken up in the middle of the night?". Their perfect response was "I like sleeping at night". If they answered with "Yeah, I really hate it.", they were considered more unstable than not.

He words it stable person, I say a good social fit. You need the right personalities to do certain jobs.

This has a bit to do with my decisions: http://old-soldier-colonel.blogspot.com/2011/07/field-marshal-moltkes-four-types-of.html?m=1

You gotta filter out that bad square. If you don't, then you waste time training only to fire.

Subject matter tests are important for skilled positions. Someone with 4 years of experience should know something. Otherwise, they've been fucking off that long.

Edit: be sure to list your successes on your resume and not just your job duties. Associate yourself with success.

I've been involved in hiring at a few places and we NEVER looked at academics or cared to. We wanted experience, and we listened to the way candidates discussed the subject matter. We passed up the "best" merited candidate for one of our positions because we didn't think their personality would work well with their supervisor and the structure of the division. It was very "top down, follow directions given", and The candidate seemed to suggest in their answers they didn't like that work style. We've also passed up people over qualified for the position because we didn't want them to leave after a month or two for better offers. When I hire I tend to go for the person who appears most genuine and engaged. They better be able to talk about our mission and they better be able to talk about their position. Right personality for the job. Different personalities excel at different things. I don't care about your people skills if you are going to primarily be alone crunching numbers most of the time.

My experience is in interviews in the electrical engineering world, but I imagine it is more or less the same in all fields.

The number one thing is, are you easy to get along with? In most of these positions, you will be interviewed separately by 3-5 different people in the group. They obviously want you to be intelligent and proficient enough to get your work done, but the main thing they are thinking is - "will I be able to stand working with this guy for 8 hours a day?" Even if you are the smartest person on the planet, if you are unfriendly and socially awkward, you will have a hard time getting hired.

For me, experience is really important. I don't really care what certificates or awards you have, I want to know what you can actually do, and I want to see some evidence that you can do it. If you are a new grad, can you tell me various projects you have worked on, or even hobbies you do on the side that are related to electronics and coding? I want employees to treat their job as a hobby that they are willing to put extra time into, because they enjoy it. I don't want people who simply got a degree and show up to collect a paycheck and have no interest in the job.

Come into the interview dressed well (i.e. dress pants and tie), and have copies of your resume, some extra paper, and a pen handy. The idea is to at least pretend that you give a fuck and are organized, which I see a lot of people fail to do.

It's not as common, but my primary criteria was personality, and then second an eagerness to learn. Most jobs are helped by previous experience, but you always need to learn a lot in a new position. Academics/certifications are just about the least important things I looked at and frequently were signs of a dogmatic and difficult to work with person.

Beyond experience, it's hard to put a finger on what I look for. Mainly I look at body language and word choice. These two things can tell you a lot about a person. If someone knows to fake what I'm looking for then they probably can handle customer service. Specifically what I'm looking for are large gestures, and an open posture. Think of the superman pose. A firm handshake, eye contact, all of that.

Word choice is a bit trickier. I don't really go into a conversation looking for this, but if someone says something that sounds odd, or uses a certain word with multiple meanings where another will do they are often telegraphing what they are thinking. When people lie, they generally tend to try and stick as close to the truth as possible.

One example of people choosing words is this: I ask the applicant to tell me about a time they overcame an challenge. If they use the word "we" and are overly general about the answer then that means that they weren't the person most responsible for the action. If they are specific and say "I" and go into detail about what they did then I'll ask about their thought process while fixing the problem. If they can walk me through that then they're pretty much hired.
I look for resourcefulness, ability to self-start, and resilience.

Been involved in hiring for years as an IT person

We generally only pay cursory attention to your academics - When we send our "job requirements" list to HR, it includes a degree of whatever level we deem necessary, and we expect the HR drones to filter out anyone missing the baseline requirements. By the time we get the stack of resumes, everyone has a degree and meets the baseline reqs, so you're not special in that light.

Primary focus is on your experience and what you've actually done. Past work responsibilities, successful projects you've worked. Certifications, if they actually mean something, can really help here (most of us have plenty of certs, we know which ones are bullshit and which ones require actual skill to attain). We'll ask you about innovative or unique ways you've solved problems before, this is generally the part of the interview where it's OK to drag out those "in the trenches nerd war stories" and tell us about the time you built out an environment of 4300 worksations in 2 months by cobbling together your own FOG server out of spare parts with no budget. Unlike you're family, we will probably understand why that's an accomplishment.

The last thing we look for is how you'll fit within our tribe. To some extent we need you to show signs that you would fit well with our environment. In some departments that means a very technical, professional attitude and the ability to work on your own - in others that means a laid back, team environment, the kind of personality that has no problem heading out to the bar after work with the rest of the group for a beer to hash out some aspect of a project. In my department (we do alot of customer facing work) I want to see that you're relaxed and personable in the interview - you should be able to talk about and explain something you are familiar with (yourself, in this case, but various projects when you're hired) to a group of virtual strangers in such a way that you can communicate your points clearly and inclusively.

Our team members must possess the technical skills to do the job, and have a desire to continue to learn and grow their skills.
